summary:
Giedrius Šteimantas opens with the story of a friend who vibe-coded a personal shopping agent: a chatbot converses with users about style, then a second agent executes purchases. Every stage used a browser automation framework, which made the system slow, expensive, and unreliable because of CAPTCHAs and access failures. Šteimantas reframes the issue as a missing infrastructure layer rather than a model-quality problem.

He introduces three principles drawn from a decade of scraping at Oxylabs: cost matters; use a browser only when absolutely necessary; and HTTP 200 does not guarantee valid content. He then dissects the friend's four-stage pipeline (discovery, decision, user confirmation, checkout) and rebuilds it.

In discovery, a fixed retailer list queried through a browser is replaced with a search API that returns compact JSON under 2,000 tokens per call with average latency under 700 ms, letting the agent fan out queries and choose its own URLs. In the decision stage, a browser-based scraper is replaced with a REST scraper API that returns markdown, runs hundreds of requests in parallel, fails loudly with an explicit error when blocked, supports geolocation, and bills only for successful results, eliminating wasted tokens on CAPTCHAs. Checkout still needs a browser, so Playwright MCP is retained but pointed at Oxylabs' hardened headless browser, which adds stealth, a residential proxy, and matching geolocation so items shown as in stock remain purchasable. He closes by reiterating that validating content before sending it to an LLM and choosing the right infrastructure layer are the key lessons.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: An HTTP 200 with non-trivial response size does not prove a page is real; CAPTCHAs still cost tokens if you feed them to an LLM.
Use a browser only when you must; discovery and decision stages usually do not need one.
Discovery benefits from a search API returning compact JSON (<2,000 tokens, <700 ms) so agents can fan out queries.
Decision stages benefit from a scraper API that returns markdown, runs in parallel, fails loudly on blocks, and bills only on success.
Checkout does need a browser, so keep Playwright MCP but pair it with a hardened headless browser offering stealth, residential proxy, and geolocation.
Geolocation matters in e-commerce: without it, items can appear in stock during discovery and vanish at checkout.
Validation must happen before token spend, not after; compression cannot rescue invalid content.
Cost matters: 70% of tokens can be wasted on blocked pages if failures are not detected upstream.
Replace a deterministic retailer list with a search tool so the agent selects its own URLs.
Treat web access for agents as an infrastructure problem, not an LLM-quality problem.

sections.title: A friend's personal shopping agent that did not work
sections.summary: Šteimantas introduces a friend who vibe-coded a chatbot personal shopper that hands prompts to a second shopping agent. Every stage ran on a browser automation framework, so the system was slow, expensive, and CAPTCHA-prone, and ultimately did not work. He identifies the root cause as a missing infrastructure layer beneath the agent.

sections.title: Ten years of scraping, and one rule: cost matters
sections.summary: He introduces himself from Oxylabs, which has spent 10 years supplying data for LLM training and now supports AI agents at web scale. He distills scraping principles into three rules: cost matters; use a browser only when necessary; and HTTP 200 does not mean valid content, since pages can be heavy with non-value JavaScript, CSS, and HTML.

sections.title: Discovery on a browser, and what it costs
sections.summary: He walks through the friend's four-stage pipeline (discovery, decision, user confirmation, checkout). Discovery relied on a fixed retailer list and a browser tool that lacked stealth, hit CAPTCHAs, was heavy in JavaScript, and could not localize results, so costs were unpredictable and items vanished by checkout.

sections.title: A search API instead: 2,000 tokens, 700 milliseconds
sections.summary: He replaces the browser-based discovery with Oxylabs' fast search API, which returns compact JSON under 2,000 tokens per response with average latency under 700 ms. The agent fans out queries, picks its own URLs from indexed search engines, and the stage runs quickly without needing a large model.

sections.title: The blocked pages you still pay tokens for
sections.summary: He explains the hidden token cost of CAPTCHAs: of 10 pages, often only 3 return valid content, but teams feed all 10 to the LLM and waste roughly 70% of tokens. Most teams miss this because they only check HTTP code and content size. The fix is validating content before any compression, not after.

sections.title: Rebuilding the decision stage without a browser
sections.summary: He rebuilds the decision stage using Oxylabs' web scraper API: a lightweight REST endpoint returning markdown, running hundreds of requests in parallel, with geolocation support. Blocks return explicit errors so the LLM never sees them, and customers pay only for successful results (no cure, no pay).

sections.title: Checkout is where you actually need a browser
sections.summary: He argues checkout genuinely needs a browser because content is highly dynamic. He keeps Playwright MCP but swaps the default browser for Oxylabs' hardened headless browser, gaining stealth at the source-code level, a residential proxy, and matching geolocation so items shown in discovery remain available at the till.

sections.title: Validate before you spend tokens
sections.summary: He closes with three lessons: borrow scraping principles when building agents, use a browser only when absolutely necessary, and validate content before feeding it to an LLM. With the proper infrastructure layer in place, teams save implementation time and token cost. Cost matters.

demonstrations: Rebuilding a personal shopping agent in four stages (discovery, decision, user confirmation, checkout) using Oxylabs' fast search API, web scraper API, and headless browser
Running hundreds of parallel scraper requests returning markdown with explicit errors on block instead of CAPTCHAs
Swapping Playwright MCP's default browser for Oxylabs' hardened headless browser to add stealth, residential proxy, and geolocation during checkout
limitations: Friend's browser-based agent was slow, expensive, and unreliable due to CAPTCHAs and access failures
Discovery via a fixed retailer list restricted item selection and could not localize stock
Browser automation without stealth triggers CAPTCHAs and breaks flow
Feeding raw HTML or CAPTCHA pages to an LLM burns tokens on invalid content
Without geolocation, items shown in stock can disappear at checkout
